title: Orchard ML — POC cost & benchmark charter
summary: Kickoff to scope a 6-week POC focused on unit economics for Orchard ML's inference stack. Discussed workload profile, success criteria (latency p95, cost per 1M tokens, throughput), benchmark plan (replay vs synthetic), batching and KV cache knobs, security requirements, and next steps to run a baseline benchmark and share cost model spreadsheet.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-04
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood CSM), Rajiv (Orchard CTO), Elena (Head of ML), Samir (Finance), Jordan (SRE)

Summary (auto): scoped POC objectives and econ guardrails; agreed on 6-week timeline; Redwood will run baseline and share cost spreadsheet; Orchard to provide traces and security constraints.

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round of intros?
[00:08] Rajiv (CTO): Rajiv here, CTO at Orchard. We're building a multi-tenant inference layer for our recommendation pipeline, looking at cost reduction and predictable latency.
[00:16] Elena (Head of ML): Elena, I lead models — want to make sure model fidelity stays the same while we bring costs down.
[00:22] Samir (Finance): Samir, Finance — I care about runway and monthly spend.
[00:26] Jordan (SRE): Jordan, SRE — networking and security constraints.
[00:30] Maya: Great, on our side Diego (SE) and Priya (CSM) — Diego will run the bench. High level agenda: workload profile, success criteria, benchmark plan, knobs (batching/caching/quant), timeline.

[02:02] Diego (SE): Quick clarification — when you say 'multi-tenant', are you expecting per-tenant isolation or pooled serving with logical isolation?
[02:12] Rajiv: Pooled serving for now; logical isolation at request level is sufficient. If we scale we might look at dedicated pools later.

[03:05] Elena: Our typical request: avg prompt tokens ~40, avg generated tokens ~220, but 25% of requests are short (<=50 tokens) and 5% are long tails >1k tokens. Peak concurrent requests around 220, sustained 120 QPS across US.
[03:35] Diego: That's super helpful. For costing we'd need the token distribution and a sample of longer tails — do you have traces?
[03:42] Elena: We can provide a one-week sample with anonymized IDs.

[04:10] Maya: Success criteria — what would success look like at the end of the POC?
[04:18] Samir: Cost target: our CFO wants per-1M-token inference spend under $120 in production assumptions. That's a hard constraint for our runway planning.
[04:30] Rajiv: Latency SLO: p95 end-to-end generation under 300ms for short to medium prompts (<=300 tokens) and graceful degradation for long tails. Also throughput target: sustain 120 QPS with less than 5% tail failures.
[04:50] Elena: Model quality must be within 1-2% of current internal evals for key metrics — we can share eval tests.

[05:30] Diego: Ok noted. For the POC plan we usually run three passes: 1) Replay your traffic on hosted Redwood to get a baseline; 2) Controlled microbench with tuning knobs (batch sizes, concurrency, KV cache policies, quantized variants); 3) If needed, private deploy trial for network/residency checks.
[05:55] Jordan: On the private deploy, we have strict egress rules. Anything that requires outbound to 3rd party needs approval, so we'd likely try hosted within a VPC peering or leverage private deployment.
[06:12] Priya (CSM): We'll capture those network constraints — that's why we asked Jordan to join.

[07:00] Diego: Regarding per-token economics, rough hosted estimates: for model X (7B FP16-ish), at our typical shapes, hosted per-1M-inference-tokens is around $90–$130 depending on batch/caching. With aggressive KV cache and batching we can push lower. On dedicated, unit cost can drop further but with committed spend.
[07:30] Samir: That's around the number we hoped for but need a breakdown — compute vs storage vs peering vs middleware.
[07:40] Maya: We'll share a cost model spreadsheet. It separates token compute, GPU amortization, networking, and request overheads.

[08:10] Elena: More on caching — how does Redwood handle prefix/KV cache for conversational workloads? We have lots of repeated prefixes across tenant groups.
[08:20] Diego: We support prefix KV caching; hit rates vary. If your prefix reuse is high, effective tokens served drop significantly. Key knobs: cache TTL, shard placement, and consistency window. For 40% prefix reuse you might see 25–40% token reduction in real workloads.
[08:45] Elena: Good. We have a few heavy hitters that could benefit.

[09:20] Diego: Batching strategy — continuous batching in the runtime aggregates across requests; important knobs are max batch size and max wait (latency budget). If you pick a max wait of 10ms and model latency is 40ms, we get decent batching without blowing p95. For lower p95 we reduce wait but lose batching efficiency.
[09:50] Samir: What's the estimated cost delta between aggressive batching and low-batch low-latency config?
[09:58] Diego: Ballpark: aggressive batching could cut per-token spend by 15–35% depending on request size distribution and model. For long responses batching helps less because generation dominates per-token compute.

[11:00] Rajiv: How do you compare hosted vs dedicated capacity economically? We are trying to see if committing to Dedicated is worth the discount.
[11:10] Maya: Dedicated is attractive if you can commit to steady baseline throughput. Typical tipping point is when your sustained monthly token volume exceeds what you'd pay on hosted after discount — our hood rule is around X tokens/month (we'll put specific numbers in the spreadsheet). Dedicated gives better predictable latency and isolates noisy neighbors.
[11:35] Samir: We need a model that shows break-even point.
[11:40] Maya: We'll include dedicated vs hosted curves in the econ spreadsheet.

[12:05] Elena: Benchmarks — Diego, how do you ensure the replay is faithful? We worry synthetic tests don't capture dependency chains we have in production.
[12:15] Diego: We do both. Replay uses your actual recorded requests including token lengths and concurrency shapes — that captures dependencies and tail behavior. Synthetic microbench isolates latency and kernel-level performance. We'll run both and correlate results. We'll also run an A/B with your internal model outputs to validate quality.

[13:00] Jordan: Security — we need SOC2 level logs, encryption at rest & in transit, KMS integration. Also we need to know where logs are stored and retention policies.
[13:12] Priya: Redwood has SOC2 and supports KMS/HSM for private deployments; we'll package an excerpt of our security docs. For hosted we can do VPC peering and private endpoints.
[13:30] Jordan: Great, please also send a network egress guide — our security team will review.

[14:10] Maya: Timeline — propose 6-week cadence: week 0 (kickoff & trace handoff), week 1-2 baseline replay and initial cost runs, week 3 microbench + knob tuning, week 4-5 optimization iteration and optional private deploy smoke test, week 6 review and handoff with SOW for next phase. Does that align?
[14:35] Rajiv: Yes, 6 weeks works. We may accelerate if traces are ready.

[15:05] Diego: Concrete deliverables from Redwood: baseline report with p50/p95 latency and token-level cost, tuning run results showing cost deltas for different batching/cache policies, quality regression checks (your eval tests), and cost-econ spreadsheet with break-even curves.
[15:28] Samir: Will we get a single number per-1M tokens for our shapes? That's what finance needs.
[15:33] Diego: Yes — we'll produce per-1M-token estimates for several config points (conservative, default, aggressive).

[16:00] Elena: One technical nit — our long tail sometimes triggers context window >4k and some models use KVM sharding; will Redwood's runtime support KV cache fragmentation?
[16:12] Diego: We do support sharded KV across GPUs and the runtime picks placement to minimize cross-GPU hops. For very long contexts we may recommend chunking or using a larger context model; we'll test both scenarios in the microbench.

[18:00] Rajiv: Can you outline failure modes and fallback policies? If the dedicated pool is saturated, we'd want graceful fallback to cheaper model rather than request drop.
[18:12] Maya: Yes we can configure smart routing and auto-fallback to smaller quantized variants or to a lower-tier region. We'll include a recommended fallback policy in the SOW.

[20:10] Samir: Pricing transparency — will the hosted runs show line-by-line token accounting?
[20:16] Maya: Yes, we can enable token-level logs, cost breakdown per route and model. That is part of Redwood Console.

[22:00] Elena: For the POC, what do you need from our side?
[22:05] Maya: Sample traces, evaluation prompt sets, network constraints, decision maker contact for procurement.
[22:12] Rajiv: We'll share the traces and set up SSO review with Jordan.

[23:00] Diego: We'll start with a baseline hosted run using your traffic shape — it's low lift for you. If that replicates production behavior well, we can iterate to dedicated testing later.

[24:00] Priya: I'll follow up with calendar invites for the security deep-dive and the kickoff artifact links.

[25:00] Maya: Recap: Redwood runs baseline replay (Diego), share cost spreadsheet (Maya), Orchard provides traces & token histograms (Elena), security deep-dive to be scheduled (Priya/Jordan).

[25:45] Samir: On procurement timeline — if POC looks good, we might sign a Q3 committed contract. Need clear numbers to present to CFO.
[26:00] Maya: We'll aim to provide the conservative and aggressive per-1M token lines so you have ranges for finance.

[27:00] Rajiv: Any blockers on our side?
[27:05] Elena: I need to check redaction of traces — we can anonymize but need to be careful about PII.
[27:12] Priya: We can accept hashed IDs and remove payloads that include PII.

[28:00] Diego: A few tech notes for the baseline run: 1) we'll replay at your observed concurrency, 2) we'll record token-level metrics and GPU utilization, 3) we'll test with and without KV cache enabled to show delta.

[30:00] Jordan: About VPC peering — what's the expected network config?
[30:05] Maya: For peering we'll share a network diagram and egress IP ranges. If peering isn't possible we can do TLS endpoint with mutual TLS.

[32:00] Samir: Can you give an example of the per-1M token split? Even rough numbers help.
[32:12] Diego: Rough (example only): hosted default config for model X: $110/1M tokens (compute $85, networking $10, op overhead $15). Aggressive batching + cache: $75/1M. Dedicated (committed) could drop compute to $50/1M after amortization, total ~$65/1M. We'll provide exacts after baseline.

[34:00] Elena: For quality checks we'll run our eval set: rank correlation and response-SIM metrics. If quality drops beyond threshold we'll rule out a config.

[35:00] Maya: Ok last bit — reporting cadence: weekly 30-min sync and a mid-POC checkpoint with a slide deck.

[36:00] Rajiv: Works for us. Anything else?
[36:05] Samir: No, just please make the cost model conservative.
[36:10] Maya: Absolutely. We'll include conservative buckets and assumptions.

[37:00] Priya: I'll drop the security doc link and the shared drive.
[37:10] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the spreadsheet.
[37:20] Rajiv: Thanks all.

End of meeting.

Notes: transcription has occasional mis-attributions and filler words — cleaned lightly.
